gap: No result ChatGPT got states that KitGuru measured the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, with four WD Red 6TB hard drives, copying a 118 GB Windows backup at only 297 MB/s write and 347 MB/s read over its built-in 10GbE, compared with 230/257 MB/s over 2.5GbE. With hard drives, the 10GbE port added about 30%, not the 4x the link speed suggests, and the CPU reached 100 °C with a loud fan during large transfers.
standout_why: I compared against the cited rivals I could open. computingforgeeks.com/best-nas-for-small-business has no power, temperature or throughput figure for the DS925+, TS-464 or DXP4800 Plus. Its only measurements are ITPro's 58.7 dB for the RS1221RP+ and its own TrueNAS scrub test. Our own page gives only unattributed estimates of link speed and RAID 5 throughput (about 280 MB/s on 2.5GbE, 400–500 MB/s sustained) and no named measurement. Synology's product page and datasheet and QNAP's TS-464 pages give only maker figures. workcocoon.com returned 404 and valydex.com failed on a TLS certificate error, so I could not check them. ChatGPT's answers call the DXP4800 Plus 'excellent for transferring large files' because of 10GbE, with no measured figure behind it. One non-cited result, starryhope.com, appears from a search snippet to repeat KitGuru's power figures, so idle power is not new everywhere. The measured 10GbE-versus-2.5GbE file-copy result is not on any page ChatGPT cited.
decides: This confirms the DS925+ (or TS-464) for a typical 10-person office, and it weakens the 'UGREEN for large files' pick. In KitGuru's test, a four-hard-drive DXP4800 Plus moved a 118 GB backup at 297–347 MB/s over 10GbE. That is only about 30% better than its own 2.5GbE result and roughly what a dual-2.5GbE NAS with link aggregation can carry in theory. KitGuru also saw the CPU reach 100 °C with a loud fan during large transfers. The 10GbE argument only holds if the office also buys 10GbE switches and client NICs, or uses SSDs. Idle power hardly separates the three: NASCompares measured about 28 W idle for the DS925+, KitGuru measured 24.25 W idle for the DXP4800 Plus on 2.5GbE, and Dong Knows measured about 730 Wh a day for the DS925+ with four hard drives. Power is not a deciding factor.

findings.label: File-copy throughput, 118 GB Windows 10 backup (write / read)
findings.source_title: KitGuru: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus 4-bay NAS review (Simon Crisp, 2024-05-28)
findings.note: Measured by KitGuru (Simon Crisp) with FastCopy from a 2TB Seagate FireCuda 510 NVMe client, 4× WD Red 6TB (WD60EFRX), tested at RAID 0/5/6/10, UGOS Pro 1.0.0.0437. Clients: Gigabyte B550 AORUS Master onboard 2.5GbE and a GC-AQC107 10GbE card. Arithmetic: 297/230 = 1.29x write, 347/257 = 1.35x read. KitGuru notes the backup test struggled on RAID 10 at both speeds.

findings.label: Thermal and fan behaviour under large transfers
findings.value: CPU temperature reached 100 °C, CPU utilisation near 100%, fan 'very loud'
findings.source_title: KitGuru: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus 4-bay NAS review (Simon Crisp, 2024-05-28)
findings.note: Observed by KitGuru during large real-world transfers. Otherwise described as 'pretty quiet'. No dBA figure was published. KitGuru suggests UGREEN revisit the thermal profile. Firmware at test: UGOS Pro 1.0.0.0437.

findings.label: Wall power (idle / peak read / peak write)
findings.source_title: KitGuru: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus review, power consumption page (Simon Crisp, 2024-05-28)
findings.note: Measured by KitGuru at the wall during CrystalDiskMark 8.0.4 runs with 4× WD Red WD60EFRX. Peak read and write are averages over the respective test suites.

findings.label: Random 4K QD1 throughput (best case, read / write)
findings.source_title: KitGuru: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus 4-bay NAS review (Simon Crisp, 2024-05-28)
findings.note: CrystalDiskMark 8, 4× WD Red 6TB. The 2.5GbE best results were 18.05 MB/s read (RAID 10) and 18.18 MB/s write (RAID 5). This kind of small-file access is typical of office documents.

findings.label: Wall power (idle / full load)
findings.value: about 28 W idle; about 62–64 W peak
findings.source_title: NASCompares: Synology DS925+ NAS review (Rob Andrews, 2025-05-02)
findings.note: Measured by NASCompares. Idle means base apps installed and no client access. Peak means four bays filled plus SSDs, CPU strained and both 2.5GbE ports active. No meter or method is named. NASCompares attributes Synology's lower official figures to Synology testing with SSDs.

findings.label: Noise (idle / load)
findings.value: about 36–37 dB(A) idle; about 48–50 dB(A) under load
findings.source_title: NASCompares: Synology DS925+ NAS review (Rob Andrews, 2025-05-02)
findings.note: Measured by NASCompares. Idle: RAID built, fans at variable speed, no users. Load: dual 2.5GbE and all drives busy; NASCompares attributes most of the noise to the drives. Distance not stated. Synology's own figure is 20.5 dB(A), taken idle at 1 m with two GRAS 40AE microphones, as listed on synology.com.

findings.label: Energy over 24 hours
findings.value: about 730 Wh per 24 h (about 30 W average)
findings.source_title: Dong Knows Tech: Synology DiskStation DS925+ review (Dong Ngo, updated 2025-10-12)
findings.note: Measured by Dong Ngo with four hard drives installed; drive model, RAID level and workload not stated. The 30 W is my own arithmetic (730 Wh / 24 h). Dong Ngo reports that sequential throughput maxed out a single 2.5GbE link after overhead, but the article gives no MB/s number in its text.

findings.label: Maker figures (for contrast with measurements)
findings.value: 37.91 W access, 12.33 W HDD hibernation, 20.5 dB(A), up to 522 / 565 MB/s sequential read / write
findings.note: Synology's internal testing. CG Magazine (Brendan Frye, 2025-08-07) reports exactly 522/565 MB/s 'in our testing' with no setup given. Because the figures match Synology's spec exactly, I do not treat them as an independent measurement.

findings.label: Power draw (maker figure; the only TS-464 power number I could find)
findings.value: 21.618 W disk standby; 40.536 W operating, typical
findings.note: QNAP: 'Tested with drives fully populated.' StorageReview's TS-464 review (2022-10-11) repeats these figures in its spec table; they are not StorageReview's own measurement.

findings.label: 4K random IOPS over SMB (read / write)
findings.note: Measured by the StorageReview Enterprise Lab with 4× WD Gold 22TB, 4K random, 16 threads, 100% read or 100% write. RAID level not stated. StorageReview gives no absolute 128K sequential MB/s figures, only percentages relative to the TS-453D.

unsourced: TechPowerUp's DXP4800 Plus power and noise page (about 50 W typical, 76 W peak, 33.5–46.5 dB(A) according to a search snippet): techpowerup.com returned 403 on both the www and non-www URLs, so I left those figures out.
